newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: FEATURE-Mauritius sells Africa-Asia crossroad dream.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Mauritius sells Africa-Asia crossroad dream.

text.p: For decades the Indian Ocean island of Mauritius has earned its keep from three main sources: tourism, textiles and above all sugar.

But this small nation of just over one million people is now looking elsewhere for its future living, driven to a reassessment by alternative holiday destinations, cheaper labour in other textile centres and fears that the European Union may not renew its preferential sugar agreement.

With its dynamic private sector, Mauritius now talks about profiting from its geographical position to become the meeting place of Asia and Africa, a staging post for goods, services and people travelling between the two continents.

"Asia is the fastest growing region in the world, Africa is the region with the highest growth potential. In between is Mauritius," says Raj Makoond, director of the joint economic council, the key private sector body.
Potential spin-offs for the island include more direct investments and tourists, helping it to remain one of the highest per capita income earners if included in the African continent.
Located 2,400 km (1,490 miles) off the southeast coast of Africa and just east of Madagascar, Mauritius has India as its closest Asian neighbour, far to the northeast.
HISTORY AS TRADING BASE, DIVERSE POPULATION BOON
Promoters of the Africa-Asia confluence idea point to Mauritius's history as a trading base for waves of colonisers, whose legacy is today's diverse population mix.

First to settle in the late 1500s were the Dutch, who named the island after their Prince Maurice of Nassau and who have been blamed for plundering its ebony forests and for killing off the dodo, its emblematic bird.
Next arrived the French, who established the sea port -- and today the capital -- Port Louis. They were followed by the British who ruled until independence in 1968.

Mauritius's cosmopolitan blend of Indian, White, Creole, Muslim and Chinese people is seen as strengthening its role as a hub, with goods from India and China already moving strongly through the country's ports.
"Our cross-cultural exposure makes us people who can be at ease with any person. We are Asian, we are African, we are Chinese," Makoond said.
SOME MACHINERY FOR HUB ALREADY IN PLACE

Businessmen point to the machinery already in place to achieve the crossroads ideal. An export processing zone set up in the 1970s has lured numerous foreign companies which manufacture goods for export and enjoy tax-free status.

In 1992 a free port development was launched -- a duty-free zone for all goods destined for re-export and on all machinery, equipment and materials imported into the zone. Zero-tax and free profit repatriation are some of the benefits.

Port authority chairman Edouard Lim Fat said 150 companies operate in the free port, which is expanding its storage capacity and is expected to have a turnover of two billion rupees ($97 million) this year.

Mauritius is also in regular talks with its neighbours through its membership of three regional bodies -- the Southern African Development Community, the Common Market for Eastern and Southern African Countries, and the Indian Ocean Commission.

The island sports a robust offshore banking sector, where many major international finance houses are represented. It also has a stock exchange of 45 firms and plans secondary markets in long bond and money securities.

A $60 million regional airline, due to kick off in mid-1998, is also being planned. It will fly to and from 10 destinations in East and Southern Africa, feeding the long-haul flights to Asia of state-owned Air Mauritius.
"We want to be the place where Africa and Asia meet," says Georges Chung, the promoter of the airline project.
CROSSROADS VISION REFLECTS DEEPER PROBLEMS

The determination to become a trade centre is at heart a response to the growing economic problems facing Mauritius, which threaten to puncture its gross domestic product growth of over five percent in the past three years.
"In textiles our biggest advantage was cheap labour. But with the opening up of Eastern Europe, we are no longer so cheap," said Michael Lim, chairman of the Mauritius Stock Exchange.
Neighbouring Madagascar's labour costs are also becoming more attractive, he said.
Mauritius's unemployment rate is estimated at over five percent and rising, from around 1.5 percent a few years ago.

With the approaching expiry of the island's preferential sugar protocol with the European Union, its biggest market, there are worries that it will not be renewed amid the global drive for free markets.
Despite relative political stability, there is widespread dissatisfaction with the government of Prime Minister Navinchandra Ramgoolam.
Since taking power in 1995 the left-wing/labour coalition government has been plagued by infighting. Polls show a steady slide in the prime minister's popularity.

"The government has just made too many blunders and promises," one businessman said. He noted that the recently-appointed finance minister is a medical doctor by profession and added: "What does a heart surgeon know about finance?"
